articles.title: Stuart Jones, a 42-year-old metal detectorist went looking for ordinary coins in an English field; he found a 400-year-old diamond ring with eight diamonds, which sold for £17,000
articles.summary: A metal detectorist who found a centuries-old piece of Tudor jewelry in a field in England had an ordinary day of searching for buried coins turn into an
articles.body: A metal detectorist who found a centuries-old piece of Tudor jewelry in a field in England had an ordinary day of searching for buried coins turn into an extraordinary encounter with history. It began as a surprise signal from beneath the surface that led to the discovery of a rare diamond ring, which was then inspected by a museum and auctioned for thousands of pounds. The historic piece has been sold for £17,000 to a new owner, nearly 400 years after it vanished. And, the discovery was made by metal detecting enthusiast Stuart Jones, 42, from Solihull, who found the gold ring near Wormington in Gloucestershire in November 2024.A routine search yields a historic findJones was searching a field when his metal detector gave him a signal and he went to investigate, the BBC reported. It didn’t take long before he knew he had stumbled on something much more unusual than the coins and objects usually found through metal detecting.The find was subsequently identified as a gold diamond cluster ring, thought to date from the late 16th or early 17th Century. When specialists examined it, they realized its historical importance more clearly.According to the Oxford Mail, the find is of particular interest to local archeology, because it was made in the Cotswolds, close to the Oxfordshire border.For Jones, the find marked the beginning of a long process of archeological recording, Treasure processing and preparations for its eventual auction.The Tudor ring owes its unique appearance to the eight diamondsThe ring tips the scales at 19.2 carats and features eight hogback diamonds in an elaborate floral setting. The unique setting makes the piece especially rare, however two of the stones are loose.The British Museum examined the ring before it went up for auction. Jewelry specialist Laura Smith studied the design and historical features and decided it was in keeping with the fashion of the period.The intricate setting reflects the fashion for prominent jewelry in the late Tudor and early Stuart periods, when wealthy people favored pieces designed to attract attention.According to the BBC, experts were drawn to the ring's unusual diamond cluster, one of the main features before it was put up for auction.Auction sale exceeds expectations at £17,000Eventually the historic jewelry went under the hammer at Noonans Mayfair and caught the eye of collectors. An English telephone bidder secured the ring for £17,000, turning Jones's unexpected discovery into a massive financial reward.The detectorist was delighted with the final auction result, which was above what he originally thought the find could achieve, the Oxford Mail reported.Jones has also decided to share the proceeds with the owner of the land on which the find was made, so that the financial benefit is shared between them.But the significance of the discovery is more than simply the money. The discovery and subsequent sale have put a spotlight on an object that had been lost and forgotten for centuries.Archeological program results in discoveryThe ring’s journey also involved the Portable Antiquities Scheme, a scheme run by the British Museum and Amgueddfa Cymru – Museum Wales.The program aims to encourage the public, particularly those with metal detectors, to report any archeological finds they come across anywhere in England and Wales. Recording such finds helps experts to record historical artifacts and understand more about Britain’s past.Also, present at the auction were 13 other finds by metal detector enthusiasts. Among them was a distinctive 17th century gold ring featuring a memento mori skull design, found in a field in Lancashire.What began as a regular metal detecting trip for Jones became a way for him to help out with historical research. The ring’s journey from a Gloucestershire field to an international collectors’ market has highlighted how chance discoveries by members of the public can return forgotten pieces of history to the spotlight.Images Courtesy: LancsLive and Noonans MayfairYou use AI every day. articles.title: An Ohio woman found her clothes and personal photographs in a dumpster after a divorce property dispute, then accused her former husband of defying court orders; an appeals court has upheld $2,280 in costs and fees
articles.summary: A divorce-related property dispute in Ohio took an unusual turn when a woman discovered her clothes, personal belongings and photographs in a recycling
articles.body: A divorce-related property dispute in Ohio took an unusual turn when a woman discovered her clothes, personal belongings and photographs in a recycling dumpster while trying to collect her possessions from her former husband's home. The discovery led to competing contempt motions after the former spouses disagreed over whether they had followed the court-approved arrangements for dividing and exchanging their belongings.In a November 23, 2026, decision in Dilts v. Dilts, the Ohio Court of Appeals, Fifth District, upheld a ruling that found the former husband in civil contempt and ordered him to pay $2,280 in attorney fees and court costs. The appellate court's judgment, available on Justia, rejected all four grounds raised in his appeal.Divorce agreement required both parties to collect their belongingsPhillip R Dilts filed for divorce from Brenda S Dilts on August 28, 2024, after the couple married in 2008. On September 10, 2024, the trial court issued an injunction prohibiting both parties from disposing of marital property through actions such as transferring, concealing, wasting or otherwise getting rid of it. The couple eventually reached an agreement on their divorce and property division. At a final hearing on July 17, 2025, both parties told the court that they had voluntarily accepted the terms and considered the division of assets and debts fair.Their written agreement, filed on July 20, provided that each would receive their separate property and collect their designated personal belongings from the other's residence by August 4, 2025. The agreement included appendices identifying the items allocated to each person.Woman discovered her belongings in a recycling dumpsterOn August 4, Phillip's brother, his attorney and another individual went to Brenda's home to collect belongings designated as his. Later that day, Brenda visited Phillip's residence to retrieve her possessions. However, she was not allowed to enter the home where her designated belongings were kept. Her daughter, Katie, was permitted inside but could not carry many of the larger items. Brenda therefore could not collect everything listed in the agreement.She later found additional items belonging to Phillip in the woods, garage and around her home and arranged for them to be returned through his brother. Around August 8, Brenda made her regular trip to nearby recycling bins and discovered several of her own clothing items, personal belongings and photographs in a recycling dumpster.Phillip had filed a contempt motion against Brenda on August 11, alleging that she had failed to return all his designated belongings. The court issued the final divorce decree on August 19, adopting their agreement as an order. On December 1, Brenda filed her own contempt motion, alleging that Phillip had prevented her from collecting her possessions and disposed of items designated as hers. She also requested attorney fees.Trial court found former husband in contemptThe trial court heard both contempt motions on January 6, 2026. During the hearing, Phillip acknowledged that Brenda had not been allowed to enter his home, that some of her larger belongings remained there and that some of her possessions had ended up in the recycling bin. On March 20, 2026, the Richland County Court of Common Pleas denied Phillip's contempt motion against Brenda but granted hers.The court found that Brenda had complied with its earlier order to the extent she could locate Phillip's belongings. It also concluded that Phillip had violated the September 10, 2024, injunction, which prohibited both parties from disposing of marital property, by discarding items designated as Brenda's while the divorce proceedings were pending. The court ordered him to pay $1,980 in attorney fees and $300 in court costs, bringing the total to $2,280.Appeals court rejects four challengesPhillip appealed without legal representation, raising four arguments. He challenged the contempt finding, the timing of the property exchange and retrieval arrangements, the court's handling of alleged financial misconduct by Brenda, and the award of attorney fees and costs. The Fifth District Court of Appeals considered the arguments together. It explained that civil contempt requires clear and convincing evidence that a party disobeyed a lawful court order. It also noted that trial courts have discretion when assessing evidence and witness credibility.The appellate judges found sufficient evidence that Phillip had prevented Brenda from retrieving her designated property and had disposed of some of her belongings in violation of the September 2024 injunction. They also noted that the trial court had specifically found her testimony truthful and honest.The court further held that reasonable attorney fees could be included as part of the costs assessed against a party found in civil contempt. Considering that Brenda had to defend against Phillip's contempt motion and file her own motion to recover her belongings, the judges found no abuse of discretion in the $2,280 award. All four assignments of error were overruled, and the appellate court affirmed the lower court's decision. It also ordered Phillip to pay the costs of the appeal.You use AI every day. articles.title: A West Virginia town has sued to save 12 historic buildings from demolition inside a national park, even as a $36 million federal project plans to restore other structures and bring in demolition crews on November 30
articles.summary: A historic railroad town in West Virginia has asked a federal judge to stop the National Park Service from demolishing 12 buildings inside New River Gorge
articles.body: A historic railroad town in West Virginia has asked a federal judge to stop the National Park Service from demolishing 12 buildings inside New River Gorge National Park and Preserve. The town wants the court to act before demolition crews arrive on 30 November. The Town of Thurmond and the New River Gorge Historical Society filed a lawsuit on 18 November in the US District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia, according to the West Virginia Record. The case names the National Park Service and Eric G. LaPrice, the park's acting superintendent, in his official role.The dispute centres on a $36 million project funded through the Great American Outdoors Act. The project aims to improve facilities and restore parts of the former coal mining town. However, federal spending records cited by the West Virginia Record show that about $750,000, or roughly 2 per cent of the total budget, has been set aside for demolition. The 12 buildings due to be removed include houses and outbuildings in Thurmond, the Prince Brothers General Store in nearby Prince, and a building used to store pool chemicals at Camp Brookside.Legal claims over preservation and review rulesIn their lawsuit, the town and the historical society accuse the National Park Service of breaking three federal laws: the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act. They are not seeking financial compensation. Instead, they want the court to declare that the agency has acted unlawfully and issue an order stopping the demolition until it completes further reviews. They also want officials to consider other options, including allowing private groups to lease and restore the buildings."Plaintiffs do not ask the court to substitute its judgment for NPS's," the complaint states, as reported by the West Virginia Record. "They ask the court to require NPS to honor its own plans and agreements, and to follow federal law, before taking irreversible action."Thurmond was once an important railway centre for West Virginia's southern coal industry. Its historic district was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1984. The lawsuit argues that plans to demolish the 12 buildings go against earlier National Park Service documents. These include a 1992 development plan for Thurmond, a 2011 general management plan and a 2022 survey of historic buildings and other resources. According to the plaintiffs, the 2022 survey found that most of the buildings examined in Thurmond had retained their historic character and needed only basic maintenance. They claim the Park Service failed to carry out the necessary repairs and later used the buildings' poor condition as a reason to demolish them.Disputes over consultation and bridge weight limitsThe lawsuit also claims that the National Park Service broke a preservation agreement signed in February 2025. The agreement required the agency to consult formally with Thurmond and other interested groups before moving ahead with demolition. Under the agreement, the Park Service had to share draft demolition plans and schedules, allow consulting groups 30 calendar days to send comments, and explain how it had considered their feedback.Thurmond officials say they were never given a complete set of demolition plans. According to the West Virginia Record, the lawsuit states that the Park Service sent out a significantly changed schedule on 13 November, only two days before the agency said the period for submitting comments would end. Local officials have also questioned whether the town's roads and bridge can safely handle the heavy equipment needed for the work. The lawsuit raises concerns about the impact of demolition machinery and lorry traffic on roads maintained by the town. It also points to the 10-tonne weight limit on the only bridge leading into Thurmond.Questions over private leasing alternativesAnother major part of the case concerns whether the Park Service properly considered leasing the buildings to private groups instead of demolishing them. The plaintiffs say the agency initially rejected this option because the park did not have enough staff, funding or a suitable programme to manage leases. However, a later agency decision allowed some buildings to remain if suitable lease proposals were received. The town and the historical society argue that the Park Service has not explained why the same option was not considered for the 12 buildings now facing demolition. The agency issued a request for lease proposals on 13 November, but none of the 12 buildings listed for demolition were included, according to the complaint.Broader $36 million restoration plansThe National Park Service approved its revised demolition plan in July 2025. Court documents cited by the West Virginia Record show that the agency accepted that demolishing the buildings would cause lasting damage to the historic district. However, it decided the wider project would not have a significant environmental impact because restoration work was planned elsewhere in the park.According to the agency's project outline, the $36 million investment will pay for new roofs, windows and shopfront repairs along Commercial Row. The work will also include structural repairs and new electrical wiring at three historic homes, new water and wastewater treatment plants, and a retaining wall in front of the Thurmond train depot. The Town of Thurmond and the New River Gorge Historical Society argue that restoring other landmarks does not give the Park Service permission to ignore the legal rules covering the 12 buildings. With the demolition contractor expected to arrive on 30 November, the two groups are waiting for the federal court in Charleston to decide whether to issue an emergency order stopping the work.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kick streamer CostaKid claims ‘equal rights, equal fight’ after viral video shows car confrontation
articles.summary: Twenty-year-old British Kick streamer Wolfi “CostaKid,” who is from Suffolk and has more than 500,000 followers across social media, is facing criticism
articles.body: Twenty-year-old British Kick streamer Wolfi “CostaKid,” who is from Suffolk and has more than 500,000 followers across social media, is facing criticism after a livestream clip appeared to show him hitting a woman inside a car. The video spread online on November 22, 2026. It shows the woman pouring water over his head before he turns towards her and becomes physical. Other people in the car tell him to stop. CostaKid later said an earlier clash involving a whip had led to the confrontation. No arrest or platform action over this incident has been confirmed.Wolfi “CostaKid” Faces Backlash After Viral Video Shows Him Hitting a WomanThe clip shows CostaKid sitting in the front of a car while a woman is seated behind him. He appears to be asking for a phone charger when she pours some Fiji water over his head. She then pulls back and says, “I’m sorry.”CostaKid turns towards her and appears to throw an object, spit at her, grab her hair and hit her several times. One passenger can be heard saying, “Costa, chill,” while others tell him to stop because it was only water.The woman then shouts at him and says he has pulled out her hair. CostaKid replies that she hit him first. The clip does not show the full events before or after the exchange.There is also another video from the same broadcast that appears to show a woman hitting CostaKid in the groin with a whip before the car incident. The full context of that earlier clash has not been independently established.The videos have drawn criticism of CostaKid’s response. Others have pointed to the earlier footage, though the clips do not show everything that happened.Wolfi “CostaKid” Explains What Led to the Livestream FightCostaKid later addressed the clips through his Instagram Stories. In a post cited by International Business Times UK, he said the earlier whip incident was the reason the situation escalated. He also claimed that he had left after that incident but was approached by the group again around 20 minutes later.He said he was told to get into the car and was assured that the women would not touch him. According to his account, the woman poured water on him after he got in. He then wrote, “So I crashed out!” and added, “Equal rights, equal fight.”These comments give CostaKid’s version of events. They do not independently confirm what happened before the car footage or explain every action seen in the clip. The woman involved has not been publicly identified in the reports reviewed, and there is no verified public response from her.The controversy has also brought attention to CostaKid’s earlier arrest in Florida. AOL reported that he was arrested in Miami-Dade County in October 2026 on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. The outlet said the charge is a third-degree felony and that his bond was set at $5,000. He reportedly spent five days in custody.That arrest is separate from the livestream incident on November 22. There is no confirmed information that he has been arrested or charged over the confrontation in the car. The available reports also do not establish whether police are investigating it.As of November 24, there has been no independently confirmed announcement that Kick has suspended or banned CostaKid over the video. Kick’s action, if any, should not be assumed unless the platform or another reliable source confirms it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A North Carolina family donated the development rights over their 55-acre farm straddling two counties, protecting pasture and forest in a fast-growing region where most of the soil is considered prime farmland.
articles.summary: Historically, as humans moved towards a more agrarian society, land became our primary asset.
articles.body: Historically, as humans moved towards a more agrarian society, land became our primary asset. It is one of the very few things that surpasses the degeneration of time, connecting generations and carrying stories, memories and livelihoods long after the people who once owned it are gone. But as cities expand and concrete slowly replaces open fields, forests and farmlands, preserving these landscapes becomes increasingly important. For many city dwellers, watching the horizon has become an endeavour. But there are some who cannot accept this change, for whom natural landscapes remain far more valuable than corporate development.In North Carolina, one family has taken a step towards ensuring that a piece of its land will remain untouched by future development, donating the development rights to protect a 55-acre farm for generations to come.According to a joint announcement by Johnston County, Wake County and Triangle Land Conservancy, the 55-acre property, known as Two Paths Farm, has been permanently protected through a conservation easement. The agreement ensures that the land's pastures, forests and agricultural character will remain preserved, even as development continues to transform the surrounding region.How the North Carolina family chose to protect its 55-acre farmThe farm, known as Two Paths Farm, belongs to Jennifer and Lane Tredway and covers approximately 55.2 acres across Wake and Johnston counties in North Carolina. Rather than selling the property or allowing it to become part of the region's expanding development, the family chose to protect its future through a conservation easement.Through this arrangement, the family donated the full value of the development rights, meaning the land can no longer be converted into residential or commercial developments. However, the agreement does not mean that the farm has to stop functioning. Agricultural activities and forestry can continue, allowing the property to retain the character it has had for years.The conservation effort also involved both counties, which contributed towards the associated due-diligence costs, while Triangle Land Conservancy will monitor the property annually to ensure that the terms of the agreement are respected.Why preserving the farm matters for North Carolina's growing regionThe importance of protecting Two Paths Farm goes beyond preserving one family's property. More than 90% of the soil on the land in question is classified as prime farmland. However, rather than being protected, the land was vulnerable to the pressures of rapid development and expansion.The farm's location makes its protection particularly relevant. The area around Zebulon has been experiencing considerable development, with residential housing and commercial projects taking over the area. By placing restrictions on future construction, the conservation agreement ensures that the property can continue to support agricultural activities rather than eventually being converted into housing or commercial spaces.There is also a larger effort behind such initiatives. Two Paths Farm lies close to two other properties already protected through Wake County's farmland preservation programme, creating a wider stretch of conserved agricultural land. The idea is not to stop communities from growing, but to ensure that growth does not come at the cost of losing every open field, working farm and natural landscape along the way.For a region where agriculture remains an important part of the local economy, preserving productive farmland is also an investment in its future. And in this case, the Tredway family has ensured that the land will remain available for agricultural use long after its present owners are gone.As the world continues to grow and cities keep expanding, it is easy to look at land only in terms of what can be built on it and how much it can be worth. But not every piece of land needs to become another housing complex, shopping centre or commercial project. Some spaces deserve to remain just as they are, allowing nature to exist without having to make room for human convenience. The Tredway family's decision is a reminder that ownership also comes with the choice of what we leave behind. By protecting their 55-acre farm, they have ensured that its fields and forests will continue to be part of the landscape for generations to comeYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: California homeowner hired a man to manage his Washington Airbnb home, but claims he lost control of the property after the manager moved in and transferred the deed to his wife for just $1
articles.summary: Imagine owning a house, paying its mortgage every month and planning to sell it, only to discover that someone else's name now appears on the property
articles.body: Imagine owning a house, paying its mortgage every month and planning to sell it, only to discover that someone else's name now appears on the property records. That is the situation Ellis Cameron says he is facing after hiring a property manager to look after his home in Washington while he lived in California.Cameron had entrusted Junior Patrick Adelbai with managing his house in Edgewood, Pierce County, and running it as a short-term Airbnb rental. But what began as a routine arrangement to look after an out-of-state property allegedly took a very different turn. Cameron told KIRO 7 News that Adelbai moved into the house with his wife, Karmaleen Issac, their two children and a dog.The homeowner says the family stayed there without paying rent, changed the locks and damaged the property. Then came an even bigger shock: a deed recorded with the county listed Adelbai’s wife as the owner of the house.“He’s a squatter and he doesn’t want to pay rent,” Cameron told KIRO 7 News.Cameron insists he never sold the property or gave anyone permission to transfer its ownership. Yet, with the disputed deed still sitting in the county's records, he says he cannot even sell the house he believes is rightfully his.A property manager allegedly moved into the house he was hired to manageLiving in California meant Cameron needed someone in Washington to take care of his property. He hired Adelbai to manage the house as an Airbnb rental, trusting him with the responsibility of looking after it.According to Cameron, however, Adelbai eventually began living there himself. His wife, their two children and a dog also moved into the property. Cameron said he was left paying the mortgage while the family occupied the house.He also alleged that the locks were changed and the property was damaged. When he approached Edgewood police for help, officers reportedly told him that the matter was a civil dispute that would have to be handled through the courts.“So he was living there for free,” Cameron said.But the situation became much more complicated when Cameron decided to sell the house and discovered that the ownership records did not reflect his name.The $1 deed that left the homeowner stunnedCameron said he first learnt about the disputed ownership when he was speaking to a real estate agent about selling the property.“I was talking to this real estate lady, and she says that house is not in your name; it’s under Karmaleen Issac,” he told KIRO 7 News.The document in question was a quitclaim deed recorded at the Pierce County Auditor’s Office on March 19. According to the report, Adelbai had signed the document, listed himself as the owner and transferred the property to his wife, Issac, for just $1.A quitclaim deed is a legal document through which a person transfers whatever ownership interest they may have in a property to someone else. However, it does not guarantee that the person signing it actually owns the property or has a valid interest to transfer.That distinction is at the heart of Cameron's dispute. He says Adelbai never owned the house and therefore had no right to transfer it to his wife.When KIRO 7 News reached Adelbai in jail and asked whether the deed was fraudulent, he denied the allegation.“No, it wasn’t,” he said. “The property belongs to my wife.”Issac did not respond to three requests for comment from the news station.Why a $1 deed could stop Cameron from selling his own houseThe disputed deed has created a problem that goes beyond a disagreement over who gets to live in the house. Cameron says he is now unable to sell the property because Issac's name appears in the county's ownership records.Real estate agent Maxwell Donaldson told KIRO 7 News that a title company would not insure the property's title because of the recorded document.“I contacted the title office, and they said... He’s not technically the owner of his own home,” Donaldson said.This matters because buying a house often involves more than agreeing on a price and signing a sale agreement. Most buyers who need a mortgage must also have the property's title checked. A title company examines ownership records and provides insurance against certain title-related problems. If there is a disputed deed that creates uncertainty about who owns the property, the company may refuse to insure the transaction.Without that insurance, a buyer's lender may not approve the mortgage. That means Cameron could find someone willing to buy the house but still struggle to complete the sale.Attorney calls the deed an apparent attempt at fraudThe circumstances surrounding the quitclaim deed have also raised questions from legal professionals involved in the matter.Josh Dabling, a real estate attorney who worked on the case, strongly questioned the document and the circumstances under which it was recorded.“To record this quitclaim deed is absolutely, in my opinion, an intent and a setup for a fraud,” he told KIRO 7 News. “This is illegal.”Another attorney reportedly asked police to investigate the deed as a possible crime. However, the department maintained that officers had already treated the dispute as a civil matter and said there was “no need for [a] law enforcement investigation.”Meanwhile, the Pierce County Assessor-Treasurer’s Office reportedly sent Cameron a letter saying it would not recognise the deed because the names did not match its tax records. Despite that position, the document remains on file with the county auditor.County auditor explains why the deed remains on recordSo why has the county not simply removed the document?Pierce County Auditor Linda Farmer told KIRO 7 News that her office's responsibility is to record documents, not determine whether they are genuine or legally valid.“We are simply the recorder of the document,” she said. “We do not assess legality of the documents.”Farmer explained that state law allows the office to record paperwork as long as it meets the filing requirements and the necessary fee is paid. The office does not conduct an investigation into whether the person submitting a document has a legitimate claim to the property.“When a document is recorded, it is permanently in the system,” she added.That leaves Cameron with a difficult legal route. According to the auditor's office, he would need to hire an attorney and approach a judge for a court order declaring the deed fraudulent. The process could take time and cost him a considerable amount in legal fees.Property manager is in jail on first-degree assault chargesThere is another development in the case. Adelbai is currently not living at the Edgewood house. Police said he allegedly shot at someone on the property on March 7. He was arrested and released, before being taken into custody again at the house a few days later.According to KIRO 7 News, Adelbai has remained in Pierce County Jail since late March and faces trial on first-degree assault charges. These charges are separate from the dispute over the property deed.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Government may link motor insurance premiums to traffic violations
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Road transport ministry is proposing a series of measures to address the problem of uninsured vehicles on roads, including introducing a single
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Road transport ministry is proposing a series of measures to address the problem of uninsured vehicles on roads, including introducing a single premium for four- and six-year insurance policies for cars and two-wheelers, respectively.Separately, the Supreme Court committee on road safety has asked the road transport and petroleum ministries to launch a pilot of the 'no insurance, no fuel' initiative at five petrol pumps each in Haryana and UP which have ANPR cameras that can identify vehicles and help verify their insurance status.TOI has learnt that the road transport ministry is also working on the plan to link premiums to traffic offences recorded against vehicle owners in the previous year. The proposed changes are aimed at encouraging more vehicle owners to maintain valid insurance coverage and improving compliance with the Motor Vehicles Act.The ministry is also examining options to revise the base insurance rates for specified vehicle categories, including electric vehicles, as part of a broader review of the existing premium structure.Insurance data show that nearly 25 crore active vehicles have valid insurance, which is around 81 per cent of the vehicles that are currently running across the country. While over 90 per cent of heavy commercial vehicles have valid insurance, it's around 88 per cent in the case of cars. Compliance is lowest at around 57 per cent in the case of three-wheelers, and it's around 80 per cent in the case of two-wheelers.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Florida politician says son's killing was not a 'freak hunting accident'
articles.summary: Carey Washington Vinson, 19, was inside his tent at a camping site near the Blackwater River in Florida when a bullet struck him in the head.
articles.body:
A Florida politician whose teenage son was fatally shot during a camping trip with friends says the shooting was an act of "malicious intent", not a "freak hunting accident".

Joe Vinson, a newly elected county commissioner in Florida, said his son Carey Washington Vinson, 19, was inside his tent near the Blackwater River in Florida when a bullet struck him in the head.

"As we understand it, some person(s) stood on the opposite bank of the river and pointed a gun at the sandbar campground, knowing it was occupied," Vinson said in a post on Instagram.

The local sheriff's office has asked the public for help in identifying any suspicious activity at the campground.

Police said they responded to an emergency call about a shooting and found the victim at a campground in Holt, Florida, with a gunshot wound to the head. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Santa Rosa County Chief Deputy Randy Tifft told US media that a vehicle was parked on the other side of the river at the time of the shooting and that witnesses saw it leave after the gunfire.

Vinson, who was recently elected as commissioner in Escambia County, issued a statement saying he needed to "correct a misimpression" that the shooting was an accident.

"This was not a freak hunting accident — not someone firing carelessly in the dark," the teenager's father said in his social media post.

Vinson said those on the other side of the river were "close enough to see the campfire and hear people talking".

"They fired shot after shot with malicious intent, and after a pause when the panicked campers screamed 'stop,' they fired another volley, then laughed as they drove away," he said.

Vinson said his son was a "thoughtful young man" studying history at Florida State University.

"He was so outgoing and athletic, playing soccer, hiking mountains, and beating the rest of us to the top of Giotto's Tower and Mount Fuji," his father said. "Most of all, he had a tender and loving heart — for his friends and family, for his girlfriend, for animals, for the marginalized."

Vinson called on anyone with information about the shooting to come forward to the police.

articles.title: Meghan Markle’s dad Thomas indicted on child porn charges in California, faces 40 years in prison
articles.summary: Thomas Markle Sr., 82, has been indicted in California, just days after he was declared mentally fit to stand trial by a Florida judge.
articles.body:
Meghan Markle's father, Thomas Markle Sr., has been indicted on child pornography charges in California, just days after a Florida judge determined that he is mentally fit to stand trial .

Thomas Sr., 82, has been charged with two counts of possession of child pornography and faces up to 40 years in prison if convicted.

The indictment was shared on X by Bill Essayli , the United States Attorney for the Central District of California, who noted that Thomas Sr. stands accused of "knowingly" possessing "35mm film negatives of sexually explicit material involving children."

"Federal law enforcement was notified last month that Markle possessed child sexual abuse material (CSAM) in the Philippines and at two storage units in Los Angeles," Essayli continued in his statement. "A judicially approved search warrant was executed and the materials were seized."

The indictment refers to several specific frames that were uncovered by the FBI and that contain "at least one image of child pornography [that] involved a prepubescent minor and a minor who had not attained 12 years of age."

Thomas Sr., who is currently being detained in Florida, "is expected to be arraigned on the indictment in the coming weeks in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles," Essayli continued.

"This is an ongoing investigation. Markle is presumed innocent until proven guilty," he concluded, while asking anyone with any knowledge of those involved with child pornography materials to contact the FBI.

It comes after a judge in Florida ruled that the former director of photography is able to stand trial, following a competency review by a psychiatrist, who found that Thomas Sr. — who was diagnosed with dementia earlier this year — has "sufficient ability to understand the nature and consequences of the charges against him."

Thomas Sr. was supported at the Tampa courthouse by his daughter, Samantha Markle, and her partner, Mark Phillips, who told Page Six that the couple was doing "not too bad."

Samantha, meanwhile, told reporters her dad was "doing great, thanks."

Thomas Sr. was set to have a preliminary hearing in Florida on Dec. 1, but now that he's been indicted in the Golden State — where investigators discovered alleged child abuse materials in a storage locker registered to his name — his case will now be heard in California.

He was taken into custody after FBI agents found material suspected of containing child sexual abuse imagery in multiple Los Angeles-area storage units that were registered to Thomas Sr.

Thomas Sr. — who has been in a wheelchair since his left leg was amputated last December — was initially released on bond back to his care home, but he was detained just days later after cutting off his ankle monitor in the middle of the night.

Following his Florida arrest, Thomas was hit with child abuse charges in the Philippines after finding himself under investigation by the Cebu City Police Office .

His son, Thomas Markle Jr., allegedly discovered child sexual abuse materials in his father's home and storage unit in the Philippines, and reported the alleged findings to the police.

Daily Mail reporters also allegedly discovered similar materials in Thomas Sr.'s abandoned storage near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico.

Thomas Sr. denied his son's allegations, telling the Daily Mail in October that he paid for sex in the Philippines but did not sleep with underage girls.

Samantha, meanwhile, accused Thomas Jr. of a "revenge" scheme and vehemently defended her father.

As for Meghan, she said in a statement to Page Six that she was "deeply distressed" by her half-brother's allegations against her estranged father.

The Duchess of Sussex's mom, Doria Ragland, reportedly helped the FBI identify her ex in disturbing child sex abuse photos.

If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call the Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-330-0226.

articles.title: These North Koreans say they were spied on, beaten and jailed for being Christian
articles.summary: A new report has testimonies from hundreds of defectors who say they were persecuted because of their faith.
articles.body:
Living in North Korea, Kim Bo-bin got used to praying with her eyes open.

She found ingenious ways to keep her Christian faith a secret in the Communist dictatorship, which tightly controls how and where its citizens worship. Unauthorised displays of faith could land people in prison, she tells the BBC.

So Kim would silently mouth hymns and clap with just two of her fingers. "In North Korea, if there are three people in a room, you are being spied on. So I would only close my eyes [and pray] when I lay on the floor."

Now 44, Kim lives just outside the South Korean capital Seoul, where she fled 15 years ago.

Her testimony - of how she prayed in secret for years, and was jailed and beaten for her faith - is part of a new report documenting the experiences of 570 North Korean escapees, most of whom say they experienced or witnessed anti-Christian persecution.

Spanning five years and featuring interviews with defectors from across the country, the report by British human rights group Korea Future accuses Kim Jong Un's regime of repeatedly violating religious freedom through a system of surveillance, fear and violence. It suggests little has changed after sustained international pressure, with multiple incidents of suspected Christians being beaten and tortured as recently as last year.

North Korea maintains that it allows religious freedom in spite of years of evidence heard by rights groups and the United Nations. While churches exist in Pyongyang, they are controlled by the state and widely seen as projecting an illusion of religious liberty.

"The North Korean leader's authority is god-like," says Kang Dong-wan, professor at Dong-a University. "So they cannot allow gods whose authority is above him." Pyongyang fears that religious freedom may threaten the regime itself, he adds.

First established in Korea in the late 1700s, Christianity exploded across the north after Protestant missionaries arrived in the 1880s. North Korea provides no figures on its Christian population but the UN has referred to estimates of 200,000 to 400,000 of them practising secretly, some of whom are detained in camps.

Surveillance and control over religion, like many other aspects of North Korean life, intensified under Kim Jong Un, who succeeded his father in 2011.

Three South Korean missionaries operating in the Chinese border region were arrested between 2013-2014 and sentenced to life in prison on charges of espionage and plotting a coup. It's not clear if they are still alive, as Seoul says Pyongyang has refused to share any information about the detainees.

Pyongyang has also been cracking down on smuggled memory sticks containing South Korean-made videos of Christian sermons. In 2020, it passed a law - on Rejecting Reactionary Ideology and Culture - to block so-called "foreign influence". Owning Bibles and hosting services can now result in imprisonment, while distributing religious books or videos is punishable by death.

Lessons against religion begin as early as kindergarten for most North Koreans. Children must attend "self-criticism" sessions at school in which they are warned against "superstitions", widely understood to refer to Christianity and other faiths.

This is what Kim Bo-bin recalls being taught. The faiths Koreans have long practised - Christianity since the 18th Century and shamanism, a millennia-old practice rooted in ancestral spirit worship - were dismissed as superstitions.

Her teachers never mentioned that Kim Il Sung himself was born into a fervently Christian family, or that Pyongyang had once been dubbed the "Jerusalem of the East."

Rather, every child and adult is expected to know North Korea's foundational Ten Principles by heart. They state that citizens must hold the "firm perspective" they know of "nothing greater than the great comrades" Kim Il Sung, the founder of North Korea, his son Kim Jong Il and the ruling party. The "smallest attempt" to dent this authority must not be tolerated, it adds.

The report documents both the indoctrination as well as the constant surveillance, with police and a network of neighbourhood spies monitoring suspicious activities. A former police informant says she was instructed to gather information on neighbours' worshipping, and handed a memo by an officer describing Christianity as an "anti-socialist activity".

North Korean authorities are also reported to hold intergenerational records of families' beliefs condemning Christians' children and grandchildren to a life without higher education or decent career prospects.

All of this illustrates how various North Korean institutions, including schools and the police, control its citizens' beliefs from "cradle to the grave," co-author James Burt says.

And yet many North Koreans turn to religion because their lives are so precarious, he adds. Faith offers them something that the state ideology "with its rigid doctrines and disconnect from their lived realities" cannot.

Kim Bo-bin grew up in North Hamgyong province, along the border with China. It was a remote, impoverished part of the country where those deemed "untrustworthy" by the state ended up, such as landowners and Christians.

Stuck at the bottom of a state-enforced hierarchy, this "hostile class" had little chance of moving up the ladder. Many of Kim's neighbours were barred from higher education and government positions, or ever living in Pyongyang.

One of them was an exiled "crazy grandma" who used to disappear into a coal shed every morning to chant words 10-year-old Kim didn't recognise. "One day, [the grandma] told me we go from ashes to ashes and dust to dust," she recalls. It was only 12 years later, when she encountered a Bible for the first time in her life that she realised the grandma was a Christian.

When a devastating famine began in the late 1990s, North Hamgyong was one of the first regions to starve because it was cut off from the state's food supply which prioritised Pyongyang. Millions were killed in what the regime described euphemistically as the "Arduous March". It was a time when many North Koreans crossed into China seeking food and work.

Kim was one of them. Aged 22 in 2003, she took what she believed was a job opportunity in China offered by a friend's aunt. But once she crossed the border, she was forced into marriage with a Chinese man and became pregnant.

While picking up a free pram for her newborn daughter at a building adorned with a cross, she encountered a missionary for the first time. Kim would join a growing group of people who discovered Christianity in China - a group that Pyongyang saw as a threat when they were returned to the North, according to Prof Kang.

Kim was arrested in China in 2007 and deported. During interrogation, she says North Korean secret police asked her if she'd ever worn a cross on her neck. She pretended not to understand. She told the police she only recognised the symbol from hospital buildings.

Kim Bo-bin says it was God's blessing the interrogator seemed more interested in whether she intended to flee to South Korea, a grave offence. She says she was beaten for 23 days and sentenced to three years of hard labour at a prison. Her story tallies with multiple accounts in Korea Future's report of extreme police violence causing broken bones and severe bleeding.

Lee Young-joo, who Kim Bo-bin met in prison also after being deported from China, tells the BBC she was interrogated about whether she'd met any missionaries, been to a church or seen a Bible. "Of course you must deny all of it. I said no, I haven't seen it," she told them.

In her prison cell, Lee says she'd keep her eyes open, begging God to save her life. Whenever anyone shut their eyes, guards would swear and shout: "Are you praying?"

Lee is glad she wasn't found to be a Christian, because she says she "would have been sent to a political prisoners' camp. I would be tortured and never allowed to leave and be buried there." This is a widely-held fear among defectors, although Korea Future's report did not hear any first-hand testimonies of Christians being held in such camps.

Lee, who previously shared with the BBC the abuse she suffered inside prison, says she was sentenced to three-and-half years. Outside of hard labour, she would spend time praying, sometimes with other Christian inmates. They would hold hands and whisper Bible verses from memory.

She and Kim Bo-bin eventually returned home after serving their sentences, where they continued to practise their religion in secret, they tell the BBC.

Kim says she managed to convert her younger sister and other relatives: "My aunt's walls are thick. The neighbours can't hear us so I quietly taught them hymns and about the all-knowing and all-powerful God."

Lee tells the BBC her mother was horrified when she learned of her Christian faith. Undeterred, she told her that she would escape again to join her daughter, who had been left in China as Lee was arrested and deported. When her mother protested, she responded saying they could all live together later.

Her incredulous mother asked: where? "In heaven," she replied.

Today, Lee attends a small church of North Korean escapees in Seoul. She prays daily, to thank God for the chicken soup and the stroll along the river. She prays for her daughter, who escaped with her in 2010, to find a nice Christian man to marry. Her mother died in North Korea some years after her escape, she was told.

Kim managed to flee to South Korea eventually, in 2012, at the age of 30, along with her daughter. She prays throughout the day - and not silently. At church on Sundays, she is the loudest singer.

articles.title: Flights to O'Hare delayed amid Thanksgiving rush, FAA says; snow possible Wednesday
articles.summary: Flights to O'Hare airport were delayed Tuesday after an equipment outage caused a ground stop Tuesday, the FAA said.
articles.body:
Flights to Chicago's O'Hare airport were delayed Tuesday afternoon after an equipment outage caused a ground stop, the Federal Aviation Administration said.

The FAA said departures were grounded due to "equipment outage."

By 4:07 p.m. the FAA said the ground stop was lifted; flights were delayed 47 minutes on average.

The ground stop only impacted flights scheduled to take off for O'Hare; flights leaving Chicago were still taking off.

In a statement, the FAA said, "The FAA is no longer under a ground stop at Chicago O'Hare International Airport but is temporarily delaying some flights while technicians work to repair a piece of air traffic equipment. The issue is specific to O'Hare, and it does not impact all flights nor affect any other airports or FAA systems."

This is the second ground stop at O'Hare airport this week.

The Thanksgiving travel rush began Tuesday at Chicago's two major airports, with officials expecting more than 2 million passengers to pass through O'Hare and Midway during the holiday travel period.

Travelers headed to the airports were urged to allow extra time for both driving and air travel. AAA projected the heaviest outbound road traffic between 2 and 8 p.m. Tuesday, and from noon to 7 p.m. Wednesday.

Watch the latest 7-day outlook from the ABC7 Weather Team.

A developing storm is expected to bring heavy rain, powerful winds and coastal flooding to parts of the East Coast on Wednesday and Thanksgiving Day, threatening holiday travel and creating potentially dangerous conditions.

Significant snow is also possible Wednesday as far north and east as the Interstate 39 corridor near Rockford.

The busy travel period follows several recent disruptions affecting major airlines and airports. After a week of outages and ground stops, some travelers said they were concerned about possible delays.

"I saw yesterday there was a stop at O'Hare, I was like 'oh, no.' I hope it doesn't backlog the different planes and I was hoping my flight doesn't get canceled," said O'Hare passenger Daniel Ordonez.

According to the Federal Aviation Administration, a staffing issue triggered Monday's ground stop, causing flights headed to O'Hare to remain at their departure airports for about an hour and a half.

The interruption was one of several issues affecting air travel ahead of Thanksgiving. On Sunday, a computer outage delayed more than 1,600 Delta flights nationwide. Last week, United said it resolved a technology outage that delayed departures.

"What we're seeing is just strange, coincidental issues. We're well-prepared for them. We have a huge playbook that allows us to respond to anything like that. We've gotten, unfortunately, some practice over the last few weeks with all these various outages we've seen throughout the system," said Omar Idris, United Airlines' vice president at O'Hare.

Nationwide, AAA expects nearly 6 million people to fly domestically during the Thanksgiving holiday. In Chicago, city officials estimate more than 2 million passengers will travel through O'Hare and Midway from Tuesday through Monday.

"We're here at O'Hare and we're geared up for one of the busiest Thanksgiving weekends on the books, for the history of O'Hare," said Karen Pride, director of media relations for the Chicago Department of Aviation.

At O'Hare alone, the city expects nearly 1.7 million passengers, an increase of just over 7% from last year. If those projections hold, it would mark the airport's busiest Thanksgiving travel week on record. Sunday is expected to be the busiest day at both O'Hare and Midway.

Among the travelers was Hayley Porter and her 2-year-old son, Chase, an experienced young flyer.

"He has gone on 14 flights and he's going to Nashville," Porter said.

When asked about traveling with children during the holidays, Porter offered a simple strategy.

Despite the expected crowds and potential delays, some passengers said they were focused on the purpose of the trip.

"Just build time in to accommodate for your kids and just be patient and just recognize that the reason for the season is to spend time with family," said O'Hare passenger Will Grossett.

Officials also reminded travelers that stopping on highway shoulders while waiting to pick up passengers could result in a ticket of up to $164. State police encouraged drivers to use the free cell phone lots at O'Hare and Midway instead.

articles.title: US jury convicts Huawei of trade secret theft, bank fraud; escapes racketeering charge
articles.summary: A US federal jury on Tuesday convicted Chinese technology giant Huawei Technologies of conspiring to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks over its
articles.body: A US federal jury on Tuesday convicted Chinese technology giant Huawei Technologies of conspiring to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks over its business dealings in Iran and alleged theft of technology from American companies. The company was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts in a case that spanned more than two decades of alleged misconduct. However, jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge of criminal racketeering conspiracy.The verdict came after a trial lasting more than two months at a federal court in Brooklyn, New York. Prosecutors called more than 60 witnesses, while the defence called 15. Huawei and three of its affiliates faced charges including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, trade secret theft and conspiracy to obstruct justice.The company could face billions of dollars in penalties when it is sentenced next September. No individual executives or employees were tried in the case, according to a report by The Associated Press.Huawei's lawyer Brian Heberlig described the acquittal on the racketeering charge as a “profound rejection” of the government's allegations. He said the company would appeal the convictions but welcomed the not guilty verdicts on racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei's decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws,” Brooklyn US Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said in a statement.“No person or company is above the law,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said.Charges against HuaweiThe US criminal case began in 2018. Prosecutors initially accused Huawei of misleading banks, including HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas, about its business dealings in Iran.They alleged that the company concealed its activities in the country to move money through the international banking system despite US sanctions.The indictment was expanded in 2020 to include allegations that Huawei had conspired to steal trade secrets from American technology companies over a period of two decades.Prosecutors argued that the company followed a pattern of stealing intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and business partners to strengthen its position in the global telecommunications market.The prosecution also alleged that Huawei made false statements to US government officials and banks to conceal its activities.The racketeering charge, commonly used in organised crime and drug-related cases, was central to the government's argument that the alleged wrongdoing was part of a wider corporate conspiracy.“The tone was set at the top by Huawei leaders and executives who themselves engaged in criminal conduct, like lying to Congress, lying to banks, violating US sanctions and trying to interfere with the very criminal investigation that led to this case,” prosecutor Meredith Arfa told jurors during the trial.Cisco, T-Mobile, Quintel among companies namedProsecutors presented several examples of alleged technology theft involving American companies.They alleged that Huawei stole source code developed by Cisco Systems for its routers. The company was also accused of taking antenna technology from wireless telecommunications firm Quintel USA.Another allegation involved semiconductor company CNEX. Prosecutors claimed Huawei hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by the company.Jurors also watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack.In another incident, a Huawei engineer allegedly entered a Fujitsu booth at a trade show and secretly photographed a device.The earlier indictment also described an incident in which a Huawei employee allegedly removed a robotic arm from a competitor's laboratory so it could be photographed and measured.The companies identified as victims in the case included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu.Meng Wanzhou's Iran admission featured in trialThe case dates back to December 2018, when Huawei's chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou was detained in Canada on a US warrant. Meng is the daughter of Huawei's founder.US prosecutors had accused her of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's business in Iran. They alleged that the company used the arrangement to move dollars into and out of Iran in violation of US sanctions.Meng fought extradition to the US for nearly three years. She eventually entered a deferred prosecution agreement and returned to China in 2021. The US subsequently dropped the charges against her.During the Huawei trial, prosecutors presented a statement attached to Meng's agreement in which she acknowledged that the company had illegally conducted business in Iran. She did not testify in the trial. However, an HSBC banker who had met her in 2013 appeared as a witness.Huawei argued banks knew about Iran businessHuawei's defence team disputed the allegations, arguing that HSBC and other banks were aware of the company's operations in Iran and were competing for its business.In his closing argument, Heberlig accused prosecutors of relying on “innuendo and facts ripped out of context” and testimony from former employees “with a bone to pick”.He also accused the prosecution of having "cherry-picked" a handful of separate incidents to build its claim of a 20-year conspiracy.“Huawei didn't steal its way to success,” Heberlig said, arguing that much of the material allegedly stolen was already publicly available.“You can't steal a secret that isn't a secret,” he said.He said Huawei had paid billions of dollars in licensing fees over the years, with 75 per cent of the money going to US companies. The company had also reprimanded or dismissed employees found to have engaged in wrongdoing.Heberlig cited an incident involving Cisco source code found in Huawei software more than two decades ago. He said Huawei recalled routers sold in the US after discovering the copied code, offered to replace them with Cisco products and introduced stronger compliance measures.Prosecutor Arfa also referred to Reuters' reports from 2012 and 2013 that helped expose Huawei's activities in Iran."After the media started questioning Huawei's operations in Iran, so did Huawei's banks," she told jurors during her closing argument.US restrictions have not stopped Huawei's global expansionThe verdict's impact on Huawei's international business remains unclear. The company has been barred from selling equipment to US telecommunications carriers for years over national security concerns. Other Western countries, including Canada and Britain, have also restricted its operations.The US government placed Huawei on a trade blacklist in 2019, limiting its access to American technology.However, the restrictions have not significantly undermined its business, according to experts cited by Reuters. Huawei has diversified its operations and emerged as an important player in China's push for artificial intelligence.The company has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries. It continues to sell smartphones and telecommunications equipment in international markets and has expanded into chipmaking.In a statement after the verdict, Huawei defended its business practices.“Huawei has always adhered to integrity in business, upheld business ethics, respected intellectual property, and remained committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations,” the company said.“We remain focused on serving our customers and partners and ensuring continuous and stable business operations," the statement said.The case has also become part of wider tensions between Washington and Beijing over technology, trade and national security. articles.title: A New Jersey mother bought a bayfront plot in 2023 hoping her son could build a home, but neighbours opposed the plan and a zoning board rejected it by a 4-3 vote; the family has now gone to court
articles.summary: A dispute over a small plot of land overlooking Barnegat Bay in New Jersey has moved to court after local authorities refused permission for a house to be
articles.body: A dispute over a small plot of land overlooking Barnegat Bay in New Jersey has moved to court after local authorities refused permission for a house to be built on it. The property's owner, Barbara Collins, and her son, Robert Eubanks, are challenging the decision, arguing that the zoning board did not properly consider the evidence supporting their proposal.According to Shorebeat's report, Collins purchased the vacant land on St. Lawrence Boulevard in Brick Township in 2023. The family wanted to use the property for a three-bedroom house, but the plan ran into opposition from nearby residents. Some neighbours hired their own experts to raise objections during the approval process.The Brick Township Zoning Board of Adjustment eventually voted 4-3 against the application. Collins and Eubanks have since taken the matter to Ocean County Superior Court. Their complaint, submitted on November 3, alleges that the board reached an unreasonable decision despite evidence presented in favour of the construction.The proposal involved a three-storey house with 1,511 square feet of living space. It was designed to have three bedrooms and two-and-a-half bathrooms. However, the plot did not satisfy several measurements prescribed for residential properties in the township.Plot size and dimensions central to the disputeThe property falls within Brick Township's R-5 residential zone, where construction of homes is allowed. However, the land covers 4,901 square feet, slightly below the 5,000-square-foot minimum stipulated by local rules.Its depth also presents a problem. The plot has a mean depth of 26.8 feet, against the required 75 feet. The proposed building would have been positioned 10.1 feet from the property line, instead of the prescribed 20 feet.These shortcomings formed part of the family's request for zoning exceptions, commonly known as variances. Collins and Eubanks maintain that the land's unusual dimensions were already present when they acquired it. They argue that they should not be denied permission simply because the property does not conform to standard measurements.Eubanks submitted the application on September 9, last year. The board held four hearings over the following months. It rejected the proposal at the final hearing and formally recorded its decision in a resolution.Family questions how board assessed evidenceThe board accepted that the property had limitations that created difficulties for development. However, its members could not agree on whether the proposed construction would serve the objectives of local zoning rules.It nevertheless concluded that allowing the house would be harmful to the public interest because the available land was too limited for the proposed building.Collins and Eubanks have challenged this assessment in their court filing. They argue that the board did not properly weigh the evidence provided by their own technical experts.The complaint names engineer and planner Charles Lindstrom and architect Michael Melillo, who appeared during the hearings in support of the project. Both were sworn in and recognised by the board as experts.The family alleges that the board gave greater weight to objections raised by professionals representing neighbouring property owners. It claims that parts of their evidence were challenged during the proceedings. The complaint also questions public comments made against the project, arguing that some did not match the evidence presented at the hearings.Offers to buy neighbouring land also citedThe complaint says Collins and Eubanks had considered ways to address the plot's limited area before the hearings took place.They approached the owners of two nearby properties with offers to purchase either their entire plots or portions of them. Such an arrangement could have increased the size of the family's land and helped it meet the minimum area requirement.The family also proposed another option. If the neighbours did not want to sell, Collins was willing to put her own property on the market at its fair value, according to the complaint.However, the efforts did not lead to an agreement. One neighbouring owner turned down the offer in writing, while the other did not reply.The plaintiffs have also brought up a separate approval they received from the state. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection issued a coastal development permit for the property on December 9, 2024, the complaint states.They have referred to this permit while questioning the zoning board's refusal to allow the project.What Collins and Eubanks want from courtThe lawsuit raises two legal claims. The first challenges the zoning board's rejection and seeks to have the decision overturned.The second concerns inverse condemnation. This legal claim applies to situations in which government action effectively deprives a property owner of the use or value of private land, even though the government has not formally taken possession of it.Collins and Eubanks argue that preventing them from building on the property amounts to such a taking. They are seeking compensation on this basis.Their main request is for the court to reverse the board's decision and send the application back with directions to grant the necessary zoning exceptions. They have also asked for reimbursement of their legal expenses and court costs.The lawsuit now places the board's handling of the application and its reasons for rejecting the proposed home before the Ocean County Superior Court.You use AI every day. articles.title: Households braced for soaring energy bills with new price cap to be announced
articles.summary: Domestic gas prices will rise significantly in January under regulator Ofgem's new price cap.
articles.body:
Domestic energy bills are expected to soar in January for millions of households, with regulator Ofgem to announce the precise increase shortly.

A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, in a forecast made ahead of the official announcement.

Ofgem's new cap, which sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, will come into force at the coldest time of year. Customers pay for what they use and charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.

The government will make a £100 payment to millions of households to help cover winter costs, in addition to an ongoing VAT cut on electricity.

The warm home discount will also take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.

"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice.

"Every day our advisers see people whose budgets have been completely wiped out by years of compounding crises. Millions of households are entering the coldest months of the year with nothing left."

Energy bills will soar - here's how you can ease the pain

Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?

About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap. Those on fixed tariffs will be unaffected, but the impact may be felt when that tariff expires and the replacement is more expensive.

If forecasts prove correct, then a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity and paying by direct debit will see a bill rise of about £37 a month from January to the end of March. If sustained for a year, it would mean the typical annual bill will rise by £443 to £2,166 compared with the current cap.

However, individual usage differs, so for every £100 spent on energy now, the new cost is likely to be about £126.

Wholesale gas prices are the dominant driver of the forecast higher prices. The war in Iran has led to higher international gas prices. With storage levels relatively low ahead of the winter, suppliers had to buy ahead at steeply higher prices.

The average price of gas is 166% higher than late last year, before the Iran war began, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK.

Andrew Sissons, from research foundation Nesta, said that the expected change in bills for households could have a wider impact.

"Higher energy bills will reduce household spending on everything else, which will have a knock-on effect across the rest of the economy," he said.

On Sunday, Chris O'Shea, the boss of British Gas owner Centrica, told the BBC he was "hugely concerned" about the impact of the January rise in prices.

There was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, he said, with some unable to pay, and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".

Energy UK calculations suggest that £67 of the average annual energy bill covers the cost of this debt. Those who pay their bill every three months, rather than by monthly direct debit, face the biggest addition.

Total energy debt was likely to rise towards £7bn by the end of the year, the trade body said.

Predictions suggest domestic energy prices could stay high throughout next year.

Even if wholesale gas prices were to fall, then network costs for running and upgrading the electricity system are expected to be high.

The government has temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about £45 a year.

The £100 support payment will be made, automatically, to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with equivalent payments in Scotland and Wales.

But Citizens Advice said that those on prepayment meters in particular, who often top up the most during the coldest months, would see the money disappear quickly.

It said it was bracing for a wave of more people seeking emergency help this winter, because they could not top up their meters

articles.body: Kilmar Ábrego García, the illegal immigrant from El Salvador who became a rallying point for critics of President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement policies, will voluntarily leave the United States for Spain to avoid deportation, Fox News has learned. articles.title: Iran to execute 2 anti-regime protesters at dawn after 3 days in death row holding cells
articles.summary: Iran Human Rights urges UN intervention as two political prisoners await execution at Ghezel Hesar Prison in Iran's high-profile "Ekbatan case."
articles.body: Two Iranian anti-regime protesters face execution within hours after spending three days in pre-execution holding cells at Ghezel Hesar Prison, according to a human rights organization warning that the men were sentenced to death following torture, forced confessions and unfair trials. Milad Armoun, 27, and Navid Najaran, 34, are scheduled to be executed in the early hours of Wednesday, Nov. 25, according to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO). The men were transferred to solitary confinement on Nov. 21 after Iran's Supreme Court upheld their death sentences. IRANIAN BOXER ON DEATH ROW WINS HUMAN RIGHTS AWARD AS ATHLETES PUSH TO SAVE HIS LIFE Both men were arrested during Iran's 2022 "Woman, Life, Freedom" uprising and are defendants in the high-profile "Ekbatan case," which stems from the killing of a member of Iran's Basij paramilitary force during nationwide anti-government demonstrations. Exiled Iranian crown prince Reza Phahlavi said on X on Tuesday that the execution would take place at dawn. IRANIAN REGIME CRITIC WARNS TRUMP DEAL COULD BE 'LIFELINE' FOR REGIME, CLAIMS PEOPLE ARE 'NERVOUS' "Despite being acquitted of the murder charge, Milad Armon and Navid Najjaran have been sentenced to death by "hanging judge" Abolqasem Salavati. "The execution orders for these two political prisoners have been sent to their lawyers, to be carried out at dawn on Wednesday, Azar 4." "Milad and Navid were held in Ward 33 which houses those accused of murder before being transferred to solitary confinement in preparation for their executions today," a source told IHRNGO. The men were sentenced to death in May by Branch 15 of Tehran's Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Abolqasem Salavati, on charges of efsad-fil-arz , or "corruption on earth," a capital offense under Iranian law. Salavati has faced longstanding criticism from human rights organizations over his handling of political cases and the harsh sentences imposed on government opponents. Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of Iran Human Rights, condemned the sentences and called for immediate international intervention. "Milad Armoun and Navid Najaran were sentenced to death following torture, forced confessions and grossly unfair trials. Their executions would be an irreversible injustice and another example of the Islamic Republic’s use of the death penalty as a tool of political repression. IRAN HANGS 2 PROTESTERS IN PUBLIC, CROWD CRIES 'DISHONORABLE' AS SECURITY FIRES TEAR GAS "Strong international reactions may be the only way to save their lives. We urge the UN and all governments with diplomatic relations with the Islamic Republic to intervene immediately to stop their executions," Amiry-Moghaddam said in a statement. The Ekbatan case centers on the death of Arman Aliverdi, a member of the Basij, a volunteer paramilitary force affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Aliverdi was injured during unrest in Tehran's Ekbatan neighborhood in 2022, and died two days later. Iranian authorities accused several protesters of involvement in his death. Armoun was arrested in Tehran in November 2022, while Najaran was detained the following month in Ahvaz. Iran Human Rights alleged that both men were tortured and subjected to ill-treatment to obtain self-incriminating confessions subsequently broadcast by Iranian state media. IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY Defense attorneys also accused judicial authorities of barring lawyers from hearings, withholding case documents and obstructing appeals. Earlier death sentences tied to murder charges were overturned, and Najaran was acquitted of involvement in the killing in a separate proceeding. However, the Revolutionary Court subsequently imposed death sentences under Iran's national security laws. The death sentences of two other defendants, Mehdi Imani and Seyed Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, were overturned, and their cases referred for retrial, according to human rights organizations. The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement erupted in 2022 following the death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish Iranian woman detained by morality police over allegations that she improperly wore her hijab.
