articles.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaving U.S. today for Spain, sources say
articles.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the El Salvador native who was mistakenly deported last year, is planning to leave the U.S. for Spain on Tuesday, according to multiple...
articles.body:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the El Salvador native who was mistakenly deported last year and sent to a notorious prison in his home country, is planning to leave the U.S. for Spain on Tuesday, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter.

Abrego Garcia, whose case became an early flashpoint in the debate over the Trump administration's deportation crackdown, is set to fly to Spain on a commercial flight Tuesday, according to the sources, who requested anonymity to talk about an arrangement that has not been disclosed publicly.

The exact nature of his arrangements and the conditions of his departure from the U.S. were not immediately clear. But the federal judge in Maryland overseeing his civil legal case issued an order Friday that remains sealed.

CBS News has reached out to an attorney and representatives for Abrego Garcia.

The move by Abrego Garcia comes after the Trump administration spent months trying to deport the man, who came to the U.S. illegally 15 years ago and had been living in Maryland with his wife and children when he was detained by immigration authorities in March 2025. He was then deported to El Salvador and held for months in the country's CECOT prison, despite a previous court order barring him from being sent back to his home country. He was brought back to the United States last year to face criminal charges.

Abrego Garcia has maintained for more than a year that if he had to leave the U.S. again, he would be willing to go to Costa Rica, and designated the Central American nation as his preferred country of removal.

But the Trump administration had resisted that suggestion and instead unsuccessfully sought to deport Abrego Garcia to numerous African countries, including Uganda, Eswatini and Ghana. In more recent months, the Department of Homeland Security said it was ready to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia — part of a broader practice of sending deportees to countries in Africa.

Abrego Garcia's departure from the U.S. came weeks after a hearing before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis, who has been presiding over a civil case stemming from his deportation last year, was abruptly cancelled . The judge ordered Immigration and Customs Enforcement last year to release Abrego Garcia from immigration custody and has continued to bar immigration authorities from detaining him while litigation continued.

But the Trump administration had sought to lift Xinis' orders, which it said were the only impediments to Abrego Garcia's "prompt removal." The Justice Department said in March that the government was "ready, willing, and able" to deport Abrego Garcia to Liberia in West Africa.

Abrego Garcia's case gained national prominence last year after a top administration official acknowledged that his removal to El Salvador was an "error." Following his arrest by immigration authorities in March 2025, Abrego Garcia was among the more than 200 immigrants who were sent to El Salvador and detained at its notorious supermax prison, the Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT.

But Abrego Garcia had been granted a withholding of removal by an immigration judge in 2019, which prevented immigration authorities from deporting him to his home country of El Salvador because he was at risk of persecution by local gangs.

In April 2025, Xinis ordered the Department of Homeland Security to bring Abrego Garcia back to the U.S., and the Supreme Court said the government had to facilitate his release from Salvadoran custody.

The Trump administration ultimately brought Abrego Garcia back to the U.S. in June 2025, but only after he was indicted on federal charges of human smuggling stemming from a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee. Abrego Garcia pleaded not guilty and in May, a federal judge in Tennessee dismissed the criminal charges on the grounds that his prosecution was vindictive.

The Justice Department has appealed that decision , and arguments before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit are scheduled for February.

articles.title: Psychology says people who close their eyes while trying to remember something may be helping their brain block out distractions
articles.summary: Someone asks you to recall the name of a person you met a few days ago. You know you have heard it before, but the answer does not come immediately.
articles.body: Someone asks you to recall the name of a person you met a few days ago. You know you have heard it before, but the answer does not come immediately. You stop looking around, close your eyes and try to picture the meeting. A few seconds later, the name suddenly comes back.You may do the same when trying to remember where you left your keys, what someone said during a conversation or the details of an incident you witnessed. Instead of staring at the person asking the question, you briefly shut your eyes, as though removing everything around you will help you find the answer.This small habit has a scientific explanation. Research suggests that closing the eyes during memory retrieval can reduce distractions and make it easier to concentrate on information stored in the brain.Why shutting your eyes can sometimes make it easier to rememberWhen your eyes are open, your brain continues receiving visual information from the surroundings. People moving around, objects on a table, a television playing in the background or even someone looking at you can compete for your attention.When you close your eyes, much of this visual input is temporarily removed. This may reduce the mental effort required to monitor your surroundings, leaving more attention available for remembering something.Psychologists call this the ‘eye-closure effect.’ It refers to the improvement in memory recall that researchers have observed when people close their eyes while trying to retrieve previously learned information.A 2011 study examined why closing the eyes can improve memory. Researchers conducted an experiment involving 80 eyewitnesses. Participants watched an event and were later asked questions about what they had seen. During the interviews, some were instructed to close their eyes, while others experienced different levels of visual and auditory distraction.The researchers found that recall was significantly better when distractions were minimal. Closing the eyes helped participants remember more details, supporting the idea that reducing the mental effort involved in processing the surroundings can improve recall. The study also found that visual and auditory distractions could interfere with remembering information presented through the corresponding senses.It is not just about blocking what you seeClosing your eyes may also help when you are trying to mentally reconstruct an earlier experience. For example, if someone asks what colour shirt a person was wearing during a meeting, you may try to picture the room, the person's position and the conversation. Removing visual distractions can make it easier to concentrate on these mental images.A separate 2011 study examined whether closing the eyes could protect memory from auditory distractions. Researchers asked 60 participants to watch a staged event before answering questions about it. Some participants were exposed to background noise during the recall task, while others worked in a quiet environment. Participants were also instructed either to close their eyes or keep them open.The researchers found that auditory distraction increased the number of incorrect details participants recalled. Closing their eyes reduced this effect.Interestingly, the benefit was not limited to remembering visual information. Eye closure reduced the effect of distraction on both visual and auditory details. The researchers suggested that closing the eyes may help by reducing the general mental effort involved in monitoring the surrounding environment.Does closing your eyes actually improve memory?Research published in August 2026 examined the effect of eye closure on autobiographical memory, which refers to memories of personal experiences. Researchers compared memory retrieval with eyes closed, eyes open and exposure to visual interference. They also examined whether the type of memory cue influenced the results.The findings showed that closing the eyes improved the rated episodic qualities of recalled personal memories. Participants also reported stronger memory experiences when they were given cues that encouraged mental imagery.The researchers found that eye closure and the use of imagery-based cues could contribute separately to the experience of remembering. However, the precise mechanisms behind these effects still require further investigation.What this habit may say about the way you rememberClosing your eyes while trying to remember something does not necessarily mean you have a particular personality trait or an unusually strong memory. It may simply be a way of reducing distractions when you need to concentrate on a past experience.It is also not a guarantee that you will remember everything correctly. Closing your eyes can help with recall, but it cannot restore information that was never properly registered in the first place. Nor does feeling more certain about a memory automatically make it accurate.The next time someone asks you to remember a name, a conversation or a small detail from the past, notice what you do before answering. If you briefly close your eyes, you may be giving yourself a quieter environment in which to search for the information.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
articles.summary: The BBC speaks to three people about steps they take to keep their energy bills under control.
articles.body:
Domestic energy prices are set to soar in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.

With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?

The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.

Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.

The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000.

She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.

The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again.

To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill .

The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often.

They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend.

"On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.

Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year.

Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.

She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.

She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water.

"I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."

Around 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets.

"When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire.

"At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1."

To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries.

Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders.

Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive.

Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.

articles.title: Why tiny cars are taking off across Europe
articles.summary: Once seen as a car for elderly, rural people, tiny cars are being embraced by a younger demographic.
articles.body:
Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.

"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.

In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.

In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16. Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.

Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.

In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.

"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.

Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.

He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.

"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."

However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."

These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem.

"You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.

Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.

Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offenses. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.

"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.

This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then.

"It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.

Tiny car sales rose strongly till 2024 although they have flattened since in France with the withdrawal of subsidies for electric models.

Curiously, the arrival in this niche market of a giant competitor in the shape of Stellantis brand Citroën was actually good news for existing French manufacturers like Aixam and Ligier.

"We're specialised in this niche market and we're very good at what we do, but of course, we didn't have the communication strength of a multinational like Stellantis. They helped us to make people understand that it was possible in France to drive this product from 14-years-old, in Germany from 15-years-old. They gave a lot of visibility to our market," says Aixam sales and marketing director Tom Faget.

Aixam has invested €30m (£25m; $33m) in expanding its production capacity in France. And its sales are growing in other European countries, even as the French market slows.

Meanwhile, the competition is producing increasingly sophisticated minicars - some costing as much as a small conventional car. At Ligier, marketing director Romain Illegems says the biggest change is in who's buying them.

"We've gone from mobility that was imposed on people to mobility that people choose. Before, these vehicles were something you used because you absolutely needed to get around, because there was no public transport, or because you didn't have a licence.

"Today, teenagers are choosing them instead of scooters or mopeds, because they're safer and offer better protection from the weather. Young people now account for 40% of our customers."

There are limitations, of course. Just two seats, a maximum speed of 45km/h and no motorways. But for Selena, who rents her Ami for €60 a month, plus insurance, it's a small price to pay for independence.
